summary: Ergoloid mesylates is an oral combination of dihydrogenated ergot alkaloids historically used for idiopathic decline in mental capacity (an FDA-approved but nonspecific indication often applied to older adults with cognitive symptoms). The usual dose is 1 mg three times daily (3 mg/day), and labeling notes some patients have used higher amounts. Unlike the natural ergot alkaloids, it lacks strong vasoconstrictor activity; it has been described as a 'metabolic enhancer' and interacts with dopaminergic, serotonergic and alpha-adrenergic receptors, but its precise mechanism in cognition is unknown and its clinical efficacy is modest and debated (controlled trials, including in Alzheimer disease, have shown limited benefit). It is generally well tolerated; side effects are mild and may include transient nausea, GI upset, sublingual irritation (with sublingual tablets), bradycardia, flushing, dizziness and orthostatic hypotension. Before prescribing, clinicians should exclude treatable causes of cognitive decline.
indications: Idiopathic decline in mental capacity in individuals over 60 years of age who show signs and symptoms of an idiopathic decline in cognitive ability (the FDA-approved labeled indication)

moa: Ergoloid mesylates is a mixture of dihydrogenated ergot alkaloids. The dihydro modification removes the strong vasoconstrictor activity of the parent ergot alkaloids. Its precise mechanism in idiopathic decline in mental capacity is unknown; it has been characterized as a cerebral 'metabolic enhancer' and demonstrates partial agonist/antagonist activity at dopaminergic and serotonergic receptors and alpha-adrenergic blocking activity. Proposed effects include modest changes in cerebral metabolism and neurotransmission, but no single mechanism fully accounts for any clinical effect, and overall efficacy is modest.

preg: Ergoloid mesylates is generally not indicated in women of childbearing potential and should be avoided in pregnancy; as an ergot alkaloid class agent, use is not recommended. There are no adequate human data establishing safety in pregnancy.
lact: Use during breastfeeding is not established and is generally avoided; ergot alkaloids can suppress lactation. If treatment is needed, weigh the benefit against potential effects on lactation and the infant.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is provided in the labeling. Use clinical judgment and standard caution in significant renal impairment.
hepatic: Ergoloid mesylates undergoes hepatic metabolism; specific dosing in hepatic impairment is not defined. Use cautiously and consider lower exposure in significant hepatic dysfunction.

major: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., azole antifungals, macrolide antibiotics, HIV protease inhibitors) - may increase ergot alkaloid levels and risk of toxicity; avoid combination
moderate: Other antihypertensives or vasodilators - additive hypotension/orthostatic effects
Drugs that lower heart rate (e.g., beta-blockers) - additive bradycardia
Other ergot alkaloids or serotonergic agents - additive effects
minor: Dopaminergic agents - theoretical additive dopaminergic effects
interactions.food: May be taken without regard to food; sublingual tablets should fully dissolve under the tongue.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol may add to dizziness and orthostatic hypotension; advise caution.

missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular three-times-daily schedule; do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Experience with overdose is limited. Expected effects relate to exaggerated pharmacologic actions and may include nausea, vomiting, flushing, dizziness, hypotension and bradycardia. There is no specific antidote; treatment is supportive - manage hypotension with positioning and fluids and monitor cardiovascular status, providing symptomatic care as needed.
